summary:
Visitors in Sokoto State stand under two penal regimes at once. Nigeria's Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 applies nationally and reaches beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have invoked it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy note on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

On top of that national layer, Sokoto State operates its own Sharia Penal Code Laws, which took effect on 31 January 2001. Male same-sex activity is punished by stoning to death where the offender is or has been married, and by 100 lashes otherwise. Sexual acts between women, termed wsafa, draw ta'azir punishment of up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment. These penalties sit inside a code that the UK Home Office records as applying across all twelve northern states, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Capital sentences under the Sokoto code are not theoretical. On 9 October 2001 the Upper Sharia Court at Gwadabawa in Sokoto State convicted Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu of zina under sections 128-129 of the Sokoto State Sharia Penal Code and sentenced her to death by stoning, while her co-accused was discharged and acquitted. She appealed on 26 October 2001, and on 25 March 2002 the Sharia Court of Appeal of Sokoto State quashed the conviction and discharged and acquitted her. The case concerned zina rather than same-sex conduct, but it establishes that Sokoto's religious courts apply the state Sharia Penal Code in practice, including the capital-punishment framework the code carries for married men's same-sex acts.

Gender expression carries separate exposure. Sokoto is listed among the twelve northern states whose Sharia criminal codes apply to Muslims, alongside Bauchi, Kano and others, with maximum penalties of death for men and whipping and/or imprisonment for women for same-sex acts. Northern states also criminalise cross-dressing: Kano carries up to one year for men who dress or behave as women, and a northern Islamic court has imposed 10 lashes for cross-dressing. Whether Sokoto State itself has enacted a cross-dressing provision is not established by these sources; nationally, Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live under fear of such proposals, and their enactment is unsettled here.

No documented arrest, trial or custody case involving a trans person in Sokoto appears in these sources, and there is no record of where trans prisoners would be housed, no trans-specific unit, and no solitary or segregation practice. Where comparable cases exist elsewhere in Nigeria, placement is discretionary: press coverage of Bobrisky's 2024 imprisonment openly asked which prison the authorities would keep her in, and an October 2024 panel found that housing her in a maximum-security facility violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act.

Practical risk also comes from non-state actors. The Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states, which covers Sokoto directly.
tangentialFactors:
Sokoto's framework is one instance of a wider northern pattern. Twelve states apply Sharia criminal codes to Muslims, and the national SSMPA applies in every state regardless of religion; visitors therefore face the stricter of the two regimes wherever they are, with the death penalty available in Sokoto for married men's same-sex acts.

Enforcement against perceived sexuality is often opportunistic rather than evidentiary. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Those affected describe the SSMPA as a weaponised law producing a climate of hostility independent of its text.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing with slow or absent accountability. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, the TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Dial (February 2025) records that six months later no suspects had been charged.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation rather than replacing it. Judicial pushback does occur: Sokoto's Sharia Court of Appeal overturned a stoning sentence in 2002, and a 2024 investigative panel found a prison placement unlawful.
localsOnly:
Sharia criminal jurisdiction in Sokoto State has a documented legislative history. An interim committee report was submitted to Governor Attahiru Dalhatu Bafarawa on 13 October 1999 and a final report, with an annexe draft bill to establish Sharia courts applying Sharia law in Sokoto State, on 16 December 1999. The resulting code came into force on 31 January 2001.

Residents who are Muslim fall under the state Sharia criminal code for same-sex acts and zina, alongside the national SSMPA; the ten-to-fourteen-year national penalties remain available regardless of which court hears a matter. Women convicted of wsafa face up to 100 lashes and/or imprisonment under ta'azir.

Residents have no statutory protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and there is no recognised mechanism for gender-marker recognition in these sources. Cross-dressing offences exist in several northern states and an Islamic court in the north has imposed lashes for cross-dressing, so gender non-conforming presentation carries recognised legal risk in the region even where a specific Sokoto provision is not recorded.

Placement of a trans or gender non-conforming detainee between male and female prison sections is left to institutional discretion in Nigerian practice; the Nigerian Correctional Service Act was found to have been breached in one 2024 maximum-security placement of a first-time offender.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Sokoto State has enacted a cross-dressing or gender-expression offence is unresolved. The sources establish such offences in Kano and elsewhere in the north, and national proposals reported in 2022, but do not record a Sokoto statute or its enactment status.

No Sokoto-specific arrest, trial, detention or custody record for a trans person is documented, and there is no sourced information on where a trans detainee would be housed in Sokoto, whether any trans-specific unit exists, or whether solitary or segregation would be applied. Absence of records in these sources is not evidence that such cases have not occurred.

Whether Sokoto's Sharia penalties and the national SSMPA penalties would be charged cumulatively or sequentially in a single case is not addressed by any source here.

The 2002 appellate reversal in the Safiyatu Hussaini Tungar Tudu matter overturned a zina conviction; how readily the same appellate route would operate for a same-sex-conduct charge carrying the stoning penalty is not evidenced.
